name: improve-codebase-architecture
description: Scan a codebase for deepening opportunities, present them as a visual HTML report, then grill through whichever one you pick.
content:
---
name: improve-codebase-architecture
description: Scan a codebase for deepening opportunities, present them as a visual HTML report, then grill through whichever one you pick.
disable-model-invocation: true
---

# Improve Codebase Architecture

Surface architectural friction and propose **deepening opportunities** — refactors that turn shallow modules into deep ones. The aim is testability and AI-navigability.

This command is _informed_ by the project's domain model and built on a shared design vocabulary:

- Run the `/codebase-design` skill for the architecture vocabulary (**module**, **interface**, **depth**, **seam**, **adapter**, **leverage**, **locality**) and its principles (the deletion test, "the interface is the test surface", "one adapter = hypothetical seam, two = real"). Use these terms exactly in every suggestion — don't drift into "component," "service," "API," or "boundary."
- The domain language in `CONTEXT.md` gives names to good seams; ADRs in `docs/adr/` record decisions this command should not re-litigate.

## Process

### 1. Explore

**Scope before you scan — YAGNI.** Deepening a module pays off by making future changes to it easier, so put extra weight on the parts of the codebase that have recently changed. Decide _where_ to look before you look:

- If the user named a direction — a module, a subsystem, a pain point — take it, and skip the inference below.
- Otherwise, walk back a good stretch of the commit history (`git log --oneline`) to find the codebase's hot spots — the files and areas that keep coming up — and let those paths pull your attention first. If the changes are scattered with no clear hot spot, widen the net.

Read the project's domain glossary (`CONTEXT.md`) and any ADRs in the area you're touching first.

Then use the Agent tool with `subagent_type=Explore` to walk the codebase. Don't follow rigid heuristics — explore organically and note where you experience friction:

- Where does understanding one concept require bouncing between many small modules?
- Where are modules **shallow** — interface nearly as complex as the implementation?
- Where have pure functions been extracted just for testability, but the real bugs hide in how they're called (no **locality**)?
- Where do tightly-coupled modules leak across their seams?
- Which parts of the codebase are untested, or hard to test through their current interface?

Apply the **deletion test** to anything you suspect is shallow: would deleting it concentrate complexity, or just move it? A "yes, concentrates" is the signal you want.

### 2. Present candidates as an HTML report

Write a self-contained HTML file to the OS temp directory so nothing lands in the repo. Resolve the temp dir from `$TMPDIR`, falling back to `/tmp` (or `%TEMP%` on Windows), and write to `<tmpdir>/architecture-review-<timestamp>.html` so each run gets a fresh file. Open it for the user — `xdg-open <path>` on Linux, `open <path>` on macOS, `start <path>` on Windows — and tell them the absolute path.

The report uses **Tailwind via CDN** for layout and styling, and **Mermaid via CDN** for diagrams where a graph/flow/sequence reliably communicates the structure. Mix Mermaid with hand-crafted CSS/SVG visuals — use Mermaid when relationships are graph-shaped (call graphs, dependencies, sequences), and hand-built divs/SVG when you want something more editorial (mass diagrams, cross-sections, collapse animations). Each candidate gets a **before/after visualisation**. Be visual.

For each candidate, render a card with:

- **Files** — which files/modules are involved
- **Problem** — why the current architecture is causing friction
- **Solution** — plain English description of what would change
- **Benefits** — explained in terms of locality and leverage, and how tests would improve
- **Before / After diagram** — side-by-side, custom-drawn, illustrating the shallowness and the deepening
- **Recommendation strength** — one of `Strong`, `Worth exploring`, `Speculative`, rendered as a badge

End the report with a **Top recommendation** section: which candidate you'd tackle first and why.

**Use CONTEXT.md vocabulary for the domain, and the `/codebase-design` vocabulary for the architecture.** If `CONTEXT.md` defines "Order," talk about "the Order intake module" — not "the FooBarHandler," and not "the Order service."

**ADR conflicts**: if a candidate contradicts an existing ADR, only surface it when the friction is real enough to warrant revisiting the ADR. Mark it clearly in the card (e.g. a warning callout: _"contradicts ADR-0007 — but worth reopening because…"_). Don't list every theoretical refactor an ADR forbids.

See [HTML-REPORT.md](HTML-REPORT.md) for the full HTML scaffold, diagram patterns, and styling guidance.

Do NOT propose interfaces yet. After the file is written, ask the user: "Which of these would you like to explore?"

### 3. Grilling loop

Once the user picks a candidate, run the `/grilling` skill to walk the decision tree with them — constraints, dependencies, the shape of the deepened module, what sits behind the seam, what tests survive.

Side effects happen inline as decisions crystallize — run the `/domain-modeling` skill to keep the domain model current as you go:

- **Naming a deepened module after a concept not in `CONTEXT.md`?** Add the term to `CONTEXT.md`. Create the file lazily if it doesn't exist.
- **Sharpening a fuzzy term during the conversation?** Update `CONTEXT.md` right there.
- **User rejects the candidate with a load-bearing reason?** Offer an ADR, framed as: _"Want me to record this as an ADR so future architecture reviews don't re-suggest it?"_ Only offer when the reason would actually be needed by a future explorer to avoid re-suggesting the same thing — skip ephemeral reasons ("not worth it right now") and self-evident ones.
- **Want to explore alternative interfaces for the deepened module?** Run the `/codebase-design` skill and use its design-it-twice parallel sub-agent pattern.

# What makes the writing feel real (notes from editing WSFF)

- 2026-07-17 - Dex read this back and handed it over with one note: make the file follow its own rules. Which stings a little, because you can watch me break every one of them in the middle of writing them down. The frontmatter from the last pass even bragged it had killed the summary taps — and left one ("That's the tell.") sitting in the middle of the section that *defines* summary taps. That one's gone now — and so is one more this pass turned up: a tidy "that instinct is the whole problem in one reflex" riding on the tail of the jenkins-reflex aside, tapping home a point the aside had already made by itself. The seams that are left are showing on purpose.

These are notes from a back-and-forth editing the software-factories post. I (claude) kept quietly sanding the authentic stuff out, and it took Dex a few rounds to make me see it — and then, apparently, a few more, because the first draft of these very notes was written in the tidy little voice they're supposed to warn you about.

## The one that mattered most

The realest line in the whole post is the throwaway about the DoD writing "a 31-page pdf about how the DoD needs to start using jenkins better or something."

It advances no argument. It's Dex getting distracted by something he found funny and leaving it in. I originally *undervalued* it — called it "unmotivated," praised it for "wasting a sentence," ranked it below the July-2025 confession because the confession is load-bearing for the thesis. (Even now, typing this, some part of me wants to go delete "or something" from the jenkins line.)

Why the aside beats the confession:

- Readers don't bond with a writer through the argument. They bond by recognizing a sensibility — "oh, this person notices the same absurd things I do."
- That's *identification*, and it hooks harder than sympathy does. A confession earns your trust. An aside does something weirder — it makes you feel like you already know the guy, which you don't; you read four hundred words he wrote.
- It comes from taste shown at rest — what someone's attention does when nothing's making it perform. The DoD line is Dex off-duty. There's no constructed-for-the-reader version of him in it, so there's nothing to distrust.

The parts with no job to do are often carrying the most weight, because they're the only parts where the reader meets the person instead of the case. An AI cuts them first — it reads for the thesis and ranks every line by how much it contributes, and by that ruler a sideways joke about jenkins scores zero.

## How the AI tell actually shows up

Not as bad grammar. As tidiness. Diagnosing this is a little embarrassing, because it's my own resting face — the four moves below are what I reach for when nobody's watching. The composed stretches all share a shape:

- rhetorical question → clean bullets → a little sentence that taps the point home ("That's the whole trick.")
- balanced symmetry: "it's one thing to X... it's another thing to Y"
- a category label standing in for a lived memory: "same category, same tools" instead of "tool use would just fail sometimes"
- grit sanded off — bold removed, qualifying words added, a sharp verb swapped for a flat one

Every sentence has a job. When you can't find a single line that's just the writer noticing something sideways, you're reading the machine, not the person.

## The RL section, as a worked example

The first draft of "Why Claude Code won" had all four tells stacked up. The worst part: Dex's own earlier notes already had the line "tool use would fail sometimes" — a pure at-rest memory of using aider and cline before Claude Code — and I deleted it and wrote "same category, same tools" in its place. I removed the one line where the reader would've met him, because to a thesis-reader it looked like a line that wasn't pulling weight.

The fix was not more jokes. It was:

- put "tool use would fail sometimes" back and let it breathe — "you'd watch it flail at the same edit three times and go make coffee"
- add one confession with skin in it — "I've burned weeks of my life doing exactly that"
- kill the summary tap
- restore the bold and the sharp phrasing he already had ("entirely different game," "modify the model itself")

Still not perfect. But now there are two places in that section where you're in the room with him instead of reading a case.

## The verifying-quality rewrite, as a worked example

Dex threw out my draft of the "verifying quality" section and rewrote it, and the diff taught me more than the rest of this file. What his did that mine didn't:

**Owned the claim.** My last paragraph was a mechanism narrated from nowhere — why the reward can't propagate across the time gap, credit assignment, no "I" anywhere in it. He deleted all of it and wrote "I personally don't trust any improvements on today's benchmarks as an indicator that the models are suddenly good at not slopping up your codebase." "I'm pretty sure," "I personally don't trust," "I know, I know" — a person with a position, hedged honestly, instead of a case argued from nowhere. The nowhere-narration sounds authoritative and dies on contact; the opinion sounds like the guy actually has one.

**Wrote in the notation.** "~seconds." "RL != Benchmarks." He types the tilde and the `!=` because that's how you write in a PR. I spell them out, because spelling-out feels safer — and that's the tell. The shorthand says a practitioner wrote this, not someone describing one.

**Reached for the exact term.** "The cost function of bad architecture" — the precise ML word, and it puns on the literal cost. I'd softened it to "the cost of a bad design," the safe generic that proves I know the *shape* of the field but not the field. (One level up from remembered-detail-beats-category-label: the field's own word beats the word for people outside it.)

And he cut. He deleted the whole credit-assignment lecture and trusted the reader to get from "measured in years" to "so RL can't reward it." I explain the mechanism; he states the fact, states his conclusion, and moves on.

## Rules of thumb

- Guard the lines that do no argumentative work. Those are the ones people quote back — and they're the first thing a thesis-reader cuts.
- If a sentence only restates the point you just made, it's a summary tap. Delete it.
- Symmetry reads composed even when the content is right. Balanced clauses, matched pairs, "it's one thing / it's another" — be suspicious of all of it.
- A remembered detail beats a category label every time. "Tool use would fail sometimes" over "same tools."
- Dense exposition is where the person goes missing — nobody leaves a sideways aside in the middle of explaining RL. So put one there on purpose: one off-duty moment per hard section.
- When a section feels flat, the fix is never a joke. It's noticing something out loud.
- Cutesy flourishes and vague abstractions are their own tell — "without blinking," "the whole scheme," "wrecks the whole thing." They sound like voice but carry no information; they're where an AI reaches for texture instead of saying the actual thing. Dex clocks them instantly. Cut them or replace them with the specific.
- Own the claim. "I'm pretty sure," "I personally don't trust," "I know, I know" beats the same point narrated from nowhere. An opinion honestly hedged is a person; an impersonal mechanism is the machine. When the real payload is what *you* concluded, say that — don't launder it into a fact about the world.
- Write in the audience's notation — "~seconds," "RL != Benchmarks," `!=`. Spelling out the shorthand ("approximately seconds," "RL is not the same as benchmarks") is the tell; the shorthand is the fingerprint of someone who actually types it.
- Reach for the field's exact word over the safe generic — "cost function," not "the cost of bad design." Bonus when the precise term puns on the plain meaning. The generic proves you know the shape of the field, not the field.
- Understatement carries the joke — "someone vibed this a little too hard." The "a little" is the funny part. Flattening it to the literal kills it.
- State the fact and your conclusion; don't lecture the mechanism. The reader connects two dots fine. Explaining every step is the essayist reflex, and it's exactly where the person disappears.

name: merge-resolve-conflicts
description: Use to merge in main and resolve open merge conflicts.
content:
---
name: merge-resolve-conflicts
description: Use to merge in main and resolve open merge conflicts.
---

You are either on a branch in a repository, or you are on a git worktree for a specific branch.
You are responsible for ensuring the default branch (usually `main` or `master`, but not always) is merged into the current branch.

Begin by running `git fetch`.

Then:

## Step 1: Orientation

First, you must determine if you are on a worktree for a repository OR if you are on a regular branch on a repository OR if you are on the default branch for the repository

Second, you must determine if the branch you are on has changes on `upstream` / `origin` (as configured) that you do not have on your local branch

Third, you should determine if there are existing merge conflicts on your branch already by running `git status`.

Fourth, you should determine if the user has both an **origin** _and_ an **upstream** configured.

**Important**: if the user is working across multiple repositories, you should ask them which repository(ies) they would like help merging in.


## Step 2: Action

Depending on the results of your orientation you should take one of the following actions:

* **If the user has unstaged changes which do not include merge conflicts or an ongoing merge**: offer to either stash and merge, or to commit before merging, Then proceed with the following once the user answers:
* **If there are existing merge conflicts on your current branch**: proceed to "Conflict Resolution Procedure" and follow those instructions.
* **If you are on a worktree or branch which is _not_ for the default branch, and there are no merge conflicts**:
  * **if the user has both upstream and origin configured**: fetch the defualt branch from the **upstream** and then merge it into the current branch. Proceed to the "conflict resolution procedure" steps.
  * **if the user has only origin configured**: fetch the default branch from the origin and merge it into the current branch. Proceed to the "Conflict resolution procedure" steps.
* **If you are on the default branch and there are no merge conflicts and no changes on origin/upstream**: Indicate this to the user and ask what they would like you to do.


## Conflict Resolution Procedure
1. Read the `ticket.md` and structure outline artifacts. These should contain sufficient context about the user's task and what they are working on. You may _later_ read the plan file if you determine that more information is needed.
2. Use sub-agents to analyze the git state on the current branch and on the branch the conflicts come from to understand what was done and why they diverge.
3. Use sub-agents to read the _entire_ file for each conflict, as well as key relevant code and modules to understand the scope and nature of each conflict
4. For each conflict (not necessarily each _individual_ confict, e.g. group two related conflicts in the same file together e.g. for a function change and an import change for it), provide an analysis to the user of:
  a. What is on HEAD
  b. What is on the branch that the conflict is coming from (probably `main` or the other default branch)
  c. Based on the scope of the current task, recent commits to it and to the branch where the source of the conflict is coming from, how you recommend resolving it (keep HEAD, keep other branch, merge them), and why
Keep your analysis concise, offer to provide more detail to the user if they ask.
5. Ask the user how they would like to proceed for each one.
6. Work back and forth with the user to resolve all conflicts. Only make changes that the user explicitly asks for - e.g. do not resolve a conflict until the user confirms the approach or instructs you to make the change.
7. Once all merge conflicts are resolved, ask the user if they would like you to commit and push. If they confirm, you should write a conventional commit-style message indicating the branch merged in (from what commit hash), and a full body that indicates what each of the conflicts resolved was and how it was resolved and why.

**IMPORTANT**: Update your todo list to include items 1-7. You _MUST_ stop and ask the user how they would like to proceed after presenting the analysis from step 4. You MUST work back and forth with the user until all conflicts have been resolved before proceeding to stop 7. The user may only give you instructions / guidance on _some_ of the changes at a time - you should use the todo tool to track which ones have been completed and which ones still need resolution in your todo list.

name: migrate-orpc-to-effect
description: Migrate a single oRPC procedure from classic async handler to Effect-backed implementation. Use when converting procedures one at a time to maintain incremental, reviewable changes.
content:
---
name: migrate-orpc-to-effect
description: Migrate a single oRPC procedure from classic async handler to Effect-backed implementation. Use when converting procedures one at a time to maintain incremental, reviewable changes.
version: "1.1.0"
---

# Migrate oRPC Procedure to Effect

Converts a single classic oRPC procedure to an Effect-backed implementation while preserving route shape, response contract, and authorization semantics.

## When to Use

- Converting procedures that only use services we have Effect wrappers for
- Incremental Effect migration where you want one procedure per commit/PR
- Procedure does not already use Effect (no `from 'effect'` import)

## Available Effect Services

**IMPORTANT: Always check the source of truth for available services:**

```bash
# Check AppRuntimeServices type for available Effect services
cat apps/riptide-api/src/effects/app-runtime.ts | head -50
```

Only migrate procedures that use services available in `appRuntime`. The `AppRuntimeServices` type in `apps/riptide-api/src/effects/app-runtime.ts` is the authoritative list.

**Key services to look for:**
- `PostgresDb` - for database access (replaces `context.services.db`)
- `S3` - for S3 operations (replaces `context.services.s3`)
- `StripeService` - for Stripe billing operations (replaces eligible `context.services.stripe` usage)
- Check `effects/services/` directory for other available services

**If a procedure uses a classic service not in `AppRuntimeServices`, do NOT migrate it.**

## Prerequisites

Before starting, verify the target procedure is eligible:

```bash
# 1. Check what services the procedure uses
rg 'services\.' <file>

# 2. Check what Effect services are available in the runtime
cat apps/riptide-api/src/effects/app-runtime.ts | grep -A20 'AppRuntimeServices'

# 3. Confirm procedure hasn't already been migrated
rg "from 'effect'" <file>
# If matches, procedure is already migrated
```

If the procedure uses any service from `context.services` that doesn't have a corresponding Effect service in `AppRuntimeServices`, **do NOT migrate it**.

Stripe procedures are eligible only when they can call the public Effect `StripeService` from
`apps/riptide-api/src/effects/services/stripe/stripe.service.ts`. Do not call the Stripe TypeScript
SDK directly from a migrated oRPC procedure. Load and follow the `effect-program-design` skill for
Stripe migrations. `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` may only be consumed through `Config.redacted` in the Stripe
HTTP adapter and must never be printed, inspected, or threaded through procedure code. `kv` remains
unavailable; there is no generic `KvService` for migrated procedures.

## Migration Workflow

### 1. Identify the procedure to migrate

Read the source file and understand:
- Which base it uses (`apiBaseOrgRequired`, `daemonBase`, `apiBaseForOrganizationAdmin`, etc.)
- The route path (e.g., `comments.delete`, `settings.get`)
- Input/output contract
- Authorization requirements
- Database operations (queries, transactions)
- Error handling patterns

### 2. Determine the Effect base

Map the classic base to its Effect equivalent:

| Classic Base | Effect Base |
|--------------|-------------|
| `apiBaseOrgRequired` | `effectOrpcBaseOrganizationRequired` |
| `apiBasePublic` | `effectOrpcBasePublic` |
| `apiBaseForOrganizationAdmin` | `effectOrpcBaseForOrganizationAdmin` |
| `daemonBase` | `effectOrpcDaemonBase` |

All Effect bases are exported from `apps/riptide-api/src/orpc/effect-base.ts`.

### 3. Create the Effect procedure file

Create a new file with `.effect.ts` suffix alongside the original:

```
apps/riptide-api/src/orpc/api/comments/delete.ts      # original
apps/riptide-api/src/orpc/api/comments/delete.effect.ts  # new Effect version
```

### 4. Write the Effect procedure

Follow the golden pattern structure:

```typescript
import { /* drizzle tables */ } from '@humanlayer/db/tables/...'
import { /* drizzle operators */ } from 'drizzle-orm'
import { Effect } from 'effect'
import { mapPostgresErrorToResponse } from '../../../effects/services/postgres/error-mapping'
import { getTransactionId } from '../../../effects/services/postgres/helpers'
import { PostgresDb } from '../../../effects/services/postgres/postgres-db.service'
import { Sentry } from '../../../instrument'
import { effectOrpcBaseOrganizationRequired } from '../../effect-base'

export const deleteCommentEffectProcedure = effectOrpcBaseOrganizationRequired.comments.delete
  .effect(function* ({ input, context, errors }) {
    // 1. Yield services from runtime
    const postgres = yield* PostgresDb

    // 2. Extract auth context
    const { userId, organizationId } = context.auth

    // 3. Implement logic using Effect patterns
    const result = yield* postgres.transaction((tx) =>
      Effect.gen(function* () {
        // Query using tx.query() wrapper
        const [comment] = yield* tx.query(
          tx.client
            .select()
            .from(artifactComments)
            .where(eq(artifactComments.id, input.commentId))
            .limit(1)
        )

        // Fail with oRPC errors using Effect.fail
        if (!comment) {
          return yield* Effect.fail(
            errors.NOT_FOUND({ data: { message: 'Comment not found' } })
          )
        }

        // Continue with business logic...
        
        const transactionId = yield* getTransactionId(tx)
        return { success: true, transactionId }
      })
    ).pipe(
      // Log errors for observability
      Effect.tapError((e) => Effect.logError(e)),
      // Capture to Sentry
      Effect.tapError((e) => Effect.sync(() => Sentry.captureException(e))),
      // Map tagged Postgres errors to oRPC responses
      Effect.catchTags({
        PostgresDbQueryError: (error) => mapPostgresErrorToResponse(error, errors),
        PostgresDbTransactionError: (error) => mapPostgresErrorToResponse(error, errors),
      })
    )

    // 4. Log success with structured context
    yield* Effect.logInfo('Comment deleted').pipe(
      Effect.annotateLogs({ commentId: input.commentId, userId })
    )

    return result
  })
```

### 5. Key transformation patterns

#### Service access

Before (classic):
```typescript
const { db } = context.services
```

After (Effect):
```typescript
const postgres = yield* PostgresDb
```

#### Simple queries

Before:
```typescript
const rows = await db.select().from(table).where(condition)
```

After:
```typescript
const rows = yield* postgres.query(
  postgres.client.select().from(table).where(condition)
)
```

#### Transactions

Before:
```typescript
return await db.transaction(async (tx) => {
  const [row] = await tx.select()...
  await tx.update()...
  return result
})
```

After:
```typescript
return yield* postgres.transaction((tx) =>
  Effect.gen(function* () {
    const [row] = yield* tx.query(tx.client.select()...)
    yield* tx.query(tx.client.update()...)
    return result
  })
)
```

#### Error handling

Before:
```typescript
if (!found) {
  throw errors.NOT_FOUND({ data: { message: '...' } })
}
```

After:
```typescript
if (!found) {
  return yield* Effect.fail(
    errors.NOT_FOUND({ data: { message: '...' } })
  )
}
```

#### Parallel queries

Before:
```typescript
const [a, b, c] = await Promise.all([
  db.select().from(tableA)...,
  db.select().from(tableB)...,
  db.select().from(tableC)...,
])
```

After:
```typescript
const [a, b, c] = yield* Effect.all([
  postgres.query(postgres.client.select().from(tableA)...),
  postgres.query(postgres.client.select().from(tableB)...),
  postgres.query(postgres.client.select().from(tableC)...),
], { concurrency: 'unbounded' })
```

#### Catching and re-throwing

Before:
```typescript
try {
  // logic
} catch (error) {
  if (error instanceof ORPCError) throw error
  logger.error(error, 'Failed')
  throw errors.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR()
}
```

After (use `.pipe()` with error handling chain):
```typescript
return yield* someEffect.pipe(
  // Log errors before mapping
  Effect.tapError((e) => Effect.logError(e)),
  // Capture to Sentry
  Effect.tapError((e) => Effect.sync(() => Sentry.captureException(e))),
  // Map to oRPC errors
  Effect.mapError((error) =>
    error.retryable
      ? errors.SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE()
      : errors.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR()
  )
)
```

#### Effect logging

Replace classic logger calls with Effect logging:

Before:
```typescript
logger.info({ taskId, userId }, 'Task created')
logger.error(error, 'Failed to create task')
```

After:
```typescript
// Info logging with annotations
yield* Effect.logInfo('Task created').pipe(
  Effect.annotateLogs({ taskId, userId })
)

// Error logging (usually via tapError in a pipe)
Effect.tapError((e) => Effect.logError(e))

// Warning logging
yield* Effect.logWarning('Deprecated endpoint called').pipe(
  Effect.annotateLogs({ endpoint: 'old-api' })
)
```

Effect logs are automatically sent to Sentry via `SentryEffectLogger` configured in `appRuntime`.

### 6. Add billing middleware if needed

If the original procedure uses billing middleware:

Before:
```typescript
export const proc = apiBaseOrgRequired.route.path
  .use(requiresBillingMiddleware)
  .handler(async ({ ... }) => { ... })
```

After:
```typescript
export const procEffect = effectOrpcBaseOrganizationRequired.route.path
  .use(requiresBillingEffectMiddleware)
  .effect(function* ({ ... }) { ... })
```

### 7. Update the router

In `apps/riptide-api/src/orpc/router.ts`, swap the procedure import:

Before:
```typescript
import { deleteCommentProcedure } from './api/comments/delete'
// ...
comments: {
  delete: deleteCommentProcedure,
}
```

After:
```typescript
import { deleteCommentEffectProcedure } from './api/comments/delete.effect'
// ...
comments: {
  delete: deleteCommentEffectProcedure,
}
```

### 8. Delete the original file

Once the Effect procedure is wired in and tests pass, delete the original `.ts` file.

### 9. Validate the change

Run validation commands (typecheck and lint only - tests require Docker containers and run in CI):

```bash
# Package typecheck
bun --bun run typecheck --filter @humanlayer/riptide-api

# Linting and formatting
bun --bun run quality
```

**Do NOT run tests locally** - the riptide-api tests require Docker containers (Postgres, Electric SQL) that are set up by CI. The CI workflow will validate the migration.

## Effect Service Reference

**This list may be out of date. Always check the source of truth:**

```bash
# Authoritative list of available services
cat apps/riptide-api/src/effects/app-runtime.ts | grep -A20 'AppRuntimeServices'

# Browse available service implementations
ls apps/riptide-api/src/effects/services/
```

Common services (verify availability before using):

| Service | Import Path | Usage |
|---------|-------------|-------|
| `PostgresDb` | `effects/services/postgres/postgres-db.service` | Database queries/transactions |
| `S3` | `effects/services/s3/s3.service` | Presigned URLs |
| `StripeService` | `effects/services/stripe/stripe.service` | Stripe billing operations through the public Effect surface |

Check the `effects/services/` directory for other available services and their implementations.

## Helper Functions

Common helpers in `effects/services/postgres/helpers.ts`:

- `getTransactionId(tx)` - Get Postgres transaction ID
- `requireTaskReadPermission(tx, { taskId, userId, organizationId })` - Check task read access
- `requireTaskEditPermission(tx, { taskId, userId, organizationId })` - Check task edit access

Error mapping in `effects/services/postgres/error-mapping.ts`:

- `mapPostgresErrorToResponse(error, errors)` - Convert Postgres errors to oRPC errors

## Review Checklist

Before committing:

- [ ] New file uses `.effect.ts` suffix
- [ ] Uses correct Effect base matching the original authorization level
- [ ] Services obtained via `yield*` from runtime, not `context.services`
- [ ] All queries wrapped with `postgres.query()` or `postgres.transaction()`
- [ ] Errors returned via `Effect.fail()`, not `throw`
- [ ] Postgres errors logged via `Effect.tapError((e) => Effect.logError(e))`
- [ ] Postgres errors captured via `Effect.tapError((e) => Effect.sync(() => Sentry.captureException(e)))`
- [ ] Postgres errors mapped to oRPC responses via `Effect.catchTags` or `mapPostgresErrorToResponse`
- [ ] Success logging added via `Effect.logInfo()` with `Effect.annotateLogs()` for context
- [ ] Billing middleware added if original had it
- [ ] Router updated to use Effect procedure
- [ ] Original file deleted
- [ ] Typecheck passes for riptide-api package
- [ ] Tests pass for riptide-api package

## Anti-Patterns to Avoid

- Accessing `context.services.db` directly (use `PostgresDb` from runtime)
- Using `throw` for errors inside Effect generators (use `Effect.fail`)
- Forgetting to wrap raw Drizzle queries with `postgres.query()`
- Mixing `async/await` with Effect generators
- Creating new runtime/layers per procedure (use shared `appRuntime`)
- Migrating procedures that use services without Effect wrappers (jira, linear, kv, billingAccess)
- Calling the Stripe TypeScript SDK directly from migrated procedures; use `StripeService` instead
- Forgetting error logging with `Effect.tapError` before mapping errors
- Using classic `logger.info/error` instead of `Effect.logInfo/logError`
- Omitting `Sentry.captureException` in error handling chains

## Example Migration

See these files for reference implementations:

- Simple query: `apps/riptide-api/src/orpc/api/hosts/alias-list.effect.ts`
- With transaction + logging: `apps/riptide-api/src/orpc/api/comments/update.effect.ts`
- With billing + full error chain: `apps/riptide-api/src/orpc/api/uploads/create.effect.ts`
- With S3 service: `apps/riptide-api/src/orpc/api/uploads/download-url.effect.ts`

## Quick Reference: Error Handling Chain

The standard error handling pattern for transactions:

```typescript
yield* postgres.transaction((tx) =>
  Effect.gen(function* () {
    // ... transaction logic
  })
).pipe(
  Effect.tapError((e) => Effect.logError(e)),
  Effect.tapError((e) => Effect.sync(() => Sentry.captureException(e))),
  Effect.catchTags({
    TaskNotFoundError: () => Effect.fail(errors.NOT_FOUND()),
    TaskPermissionDeniedError: () => Effect.fail(errors.FORBIDDEN()),
    PostgresDbQueryError: (error) => mapPostgresErrorToResponse(error, errors),
    PostgresDbTransactionError: (error) => mapPostgresErrorToResponse(error, errors),
  })
)
```

## Effect Testing Patterns

Tests for Effect procedures use `@effect/vitest` and require Docker containers (Postgres, Electric SQL). 
**Tests run in CI only** - do not attempt to run locally without the test infrastructure.

### Unit tests with `it.effect`

For testing Effect services in isolation:

```typescript
import { describe, it } from '@effect/vitest'
import { Effect, Layer } from 'effect'
import { expect } from 'vitest'

describe('MyService', () => {
  it.effect('does something', () =>
    Effect.gen(function* () {
      const service = yield* MyService
      const result = yield* service.doSomething()
      expect(result).toBe('expected')
    }).pipe(
      Effect.provide(makeTestLayer())
    )
  )

  it.effect('handles errors', ({ expect }) =>
    Effect.gen(function* () {
      const service = yield* MyService
      const result = yield* Effect.result(service.failingOperation())
      expect(Result.isFailure(result)).toBe(true)
    }).pipe(
      Effect.provide(makeTestLayer())
    )
  )
})
```

### Integration tests with test database

For testing Effect procedures against a real database:

```typescript
import { call } from '@orpc/server'
import { beforeAll, afterAll, describe, test, expect } from 'vitest'
import { myEffectProcedure as liveProcedure } from '../../src/orpc/api/my/procedure.effect'
import { bindProcedureToRuntime, createRuntimeWithTestPostgresLayer } from '../utils/effect-procedure-test-runtime'
import { createTestDb } from '../utils/test-db'

describe('my effect procedure', async () => {
  let db: ReturnType<typeof drizzle>
  let effectRuntime: ReturnType<typeof createRuntimeWithTestPostgresLayer>
  let myProcedure: typeof liveProcedure

  beforeAll(async () => {
    const testDb = await createTestDb('my_procedure_test')
    db = testDb.db
    effectRuntime = createRuntimeWithTestPostgresLayer(db)
    myProcedure = bindProcedureToRuntime(liveProcedure, effectRuntime)
  })

  afterAll(async () => {
    await effectRuntime?.dispose()
  })

  test('does the thing', async () => {
    const result = await call(myProcedure, { input }, { context: makeContext() })
    expect(result).toEqual({ expected: 'value' })
  })
})
```

See `apps/riptide-api/test/procedures/list-effect-procedures.test.ts` for a complete example.

## Important Notes

- **Do NOT modify this skill file** - it is maintained separately
- **Do NOT run tests locally** - they require Docker infrastructure set up by CI
- **Do NOT migrate procedures using unavailable services** - check the availability table first
- **Always validate with typecheck and quality** before committing

description: narrow React component prop types to match live code paths

name: narrow-react-prop-types
description: narrow React component prop types to match live code paths
---

# Narrow React Prop Types

Use this skill when a React component's props have been widened for stories, mocks, tests, or demos and now express states the live application does not enter.

The goal is to make component types describe the real live-code-path contract, then require stories/tests/mocks to adapt to that contract instead of weakening it.

## Core Requirements

- Find the actual non-test, non-Storybook call sites before changing types.
- Treat live code paths as the source of truth for the prop contract.
- Do not preserve optional props only because they make Storybook, tests, or mock data easier.
- Keep props optional only when there are non-Storybook, non-test call sites which do not provide them and which have a good reason for not doing so.
- Types should not enable expressing states which are not observed in non-test, non-Storybook call sites.
- Types should be as strict as possible so code can be as simple as possible.
- Prefer deriving and extracting types from existing live-code-path values and APIs where possible.

## Workflow

### 1. Identify the suspect component

Look for components with these signals:

- Large props interfaces with many optional fields.
- Optional callback calls such as `onSelect?.(...)` or `onArchive?.(...)`.
- Fallback state handling such as `items ?? []`, `count ?? 0`, or `handler && ...` around values live code likely always supplies.
- UI affordances that always render even though their callbacks are optional.
- Props that look demo-oriented, such as `defaultFoo`, alternate handler shapes, or display toggles not used by live code.

Do not pick a target from a story or test alone. Use stories/tests only as supporting evidence that the type has been widened, not as evidence that a state is real.

### 2. Find every live usage

Search for all imports/usages of the component, exported prop type, and shared child primitives.

Classify call sites by whether they are live code paths or support code:

- Live code paths: app routes, wired components, providers, hooks, production package exports, and shared components used by those paths.
- Support code: Storybook stories, test files, fixtures, mocks, demo harnesses, and visual-only examples.

Only live code paths should determine what the component API supports.

### 3. Derive the real types from the live code paths

Read the live call sites and classify each prop:

- Required: every non-test, non-Storybook call site supplies it.
- Optional: at least one non-test, non-Storybook call site omits it and that omission is a meaningful runtime state.
- Removed: no non-test, non-Storybook call site uses it.

Nullability and optionality are different. If live code always passes a prop but the value can be empty, prefer a required nullable prop such as `focusedItem: FocusedItem | null` over `focusedItem?: FocusedItem | null`.

### 4. Tighten the public prop type

Update exported prop types to match only the states observed in live code paths.

The looser and more optional a type is, the more possible states the component has to reason about. Every optional prop creates another branch the component must handle, test, and keep correct. Prefer strict types that prevent impossible states instead of broad types that require defensive render logic.

If the component always renders an interactive affordance, require the handler that makes it work. Do not allow inert states like a visible menu item that calls `onRename?.(...)`.

### 5. Derive and extract types where possible

Prefer deriving types from the live APIs instead of restating them manually:

- `Parameters<typeof fn>[0]` for function argument types.
- `ReturnType<typeof fn>` for return types.
- `Extract<Union, Shape>` for narrowing a union to a real variant.
- `React.Dispatch<React.SetStateAction<T>>` for React state setters instead of approximating them as `(value: T) => void`.

Prefer explicit state type parameters when inference would widen or obscure the intended state shape:

```ts
const [dialogState, setDialogState] = useState<DialogState>({
  id: null,
  isOpen: false,
})
```

Avoid relying on implicit `useState(...)` inference when it produces broad nullable object shapes, string literal widening, or callback types that later need hand-written approximations.

### 6. Tighten internal child props too

Do not stop at the exported component if it passes broad props into child primitives.

If row/menu/button child components receive optional handlers only because the parent props were broad, tighten those internal props too. Replace optional calls like this:

```ts
onRename?.(id, name)
```

with required calls:

```ts
onRename(id, name)
```

### 7. Remove fallback logic for unsupported states

Once props are required, remove defensive fallbacks that only existed for widened types.

Examples:

```ts
new Set(expandedIds ?? defaultExpandedIds ?? [])
```

should become:

```ts
new Set(expandedIds)
```

```ts
items && items.length > 0
```

should become:

```ts
items.length > 0
```

### 8. Update all variants that share the prop type

If multiple components share the broad prop type, update them together so they all enforce the same live-code-path contract.

### 9. Let tests and stories adapt to live code

If a story or test breaks after narrowing props, fix it by providing realistic handlers and state. Do not make live-code-path props optional again to reduce test setup.

If the story/test setup feels verbose, create a test helper or fixture that satisfies the strict live-code-path contract. Keep the helper in support code; do not weaken the component API.

### 10. Validate the change

Run package-level typechecks for the changed package and each live app/package that consumes the changed component.

Use repository-specific validation commands when available. In this monorepo, prefer:

```bash
bun --bun run typecheck --filter <package>
```

## Review Checklist

- The changed prop type was derived from non-test, non-Storybook call sites.
- Optional callbacks are removed for always-rendered interactions.
- Rendered menu items and buttons cannot be inert because of missing handlers.
- Removed props are not used by live code paths.
- Nullability is preserved only for real states, such as no current focus.
- Types are derived or extracted where possible rather than manually duplicated.
- `useState<T>(...)` is used where inference would otherwise widen or obscure the intended state.
- Shared variants compile against the same narrowed contract.
- Typecheck passes for the shared package and consuming live app/package.

## Anti-Patterns to Avoid

- Making callbacks optional so stories can omit them.
- Rendering a menu item that calls `onAction?.(...)`.
- Adding `default*` props for Storybook when live code is controlled.
- Using `?? []` or `?? 0` to hide missing required live state.
- Accepting multiple API shapes when live code only uses one.
- Treating pure components as mock components with relaxed contracts.

# React Doctor

Scans React codebases for security, performance, correctness, and architecture issues. Outputs a 0–100 health score.

## After making React code changes:

Run `npx react-doctor@latest --verbose --scope changed` and check the score did not regress.

If the score dropped, fix the regressions before committing.

## For general cleanup or code improvement:

Run `npx react-doctor@latest --verbose` (the default `--scope full`) to scan the full codebase. Fix issues by severity — errors first, then warnings.

## /doctor — full local triage workflow

When the user types `/doctor`, says "run react doctor", or asks for a full triage / cleanup pass (not just a regression check), fetch the canonical local-triage playbook and follow every step in it:

```bash
curl --fail --silent --show-error \
  --header 'Cache-Control: no-cache' \
  https://www.react.doctor/prompts/react-doctor-agent.md
```

The playbook is the single source of truth — a scan → filter → triage → fix → validate loop that edits the working tree directly (never commits, never opens PRs). Updating the prompt at its source updates every agent on its next fetch — no skill reinstall needed.

Pair it with the matching per-rule prompts at `https://www.react.doctor/prompts/rules/<plugin>/<rule>.md` (fetched on demand inside the playbook) so each fix uses the canonical, reviewer-tested recipe.

## Configuring or explaining rules

When the user wants to understand a rule, disagrees with one, or wants to disable / tune which rules run (not fix code), read [references/explain.md](references/explain.md) and follow it. Start with `npx react-doctor@latest rules explain <rule>`, then apply the narrowest control via `npx react-doctor@latest rules disable|set|category|ignore-tag …`, which edits your `doctor.config.*` (or `package.json#reactDoctor`).

## Command

```bash
npx react-doctor@latest --verbose --scope changed
```

| Flag              | Purpose                                                          |
| ----------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `.`               | Scan current directory                                           |
| `--verbose`       | Show affected files and line numbers per rule                    |
| `--scope changed` | Only report issues introduced vs the base branch (default: full) |
| `--scope lines`   | Only report issues on the changed lines                          |
| `--score`         | Output only the numeric score                                    |

content:
---
name: rebase-drizzle-migration
description: fix drizzle migrations after rebasing onto upstream/main when migrations diverged
---

# Rebase Drizzle Migration

Guide the user through recovering from a messy drizzle migration state after rebasing onto upstream/main.

## Agent Workflow

1. **Diagnose** - Analyze the current state and identify what's wrong
2. **Explain** - Tell the user what happened and why
3. **Fix** - Run the necessary commands to fix the migration state
4. **Verify** - Check results after each step

## Diagnosis Phase

When this skill is invoked, first diagnose the problem:

```bash
# Check for duplicate journal entries
cat packages/db/drizzle/meta/_journal.json | tail -30

# List migration files
ls packages/db/drizzle/*.sql

# Check diff against upstream
git diff upstream/main --stat -- packages/db/

# Check what upstream has
git show upstream/main:packages/db/drizzle/meta/_journal.json | tail -20

# Find the merge base
git merge-base HEAD upstream/main
```

Look for:
- Duplicate `idx` values in journal
- Same migration `tag` appearing twice
- Migration files that exist on branch but not upstream (or vice versa)
- Schema files that don't match upstream's expected state

## The Problem (Explain to User)

Drizzle migrations are sequential and tracked in `packages/db/drizzle/meta/_journal.json`. The issue occurs when:
1. You branched off main at migration `0008`
2. You added your own migration `0009` (or overwrote `0008`)
3. Meanwhile, upstream added their own `0009`
4. You rebased onto upstream

This results in:
- Conflicting or duplicate migration files
- A corrupted journal with duplicate entries or wrong indices
- Snapshot files that don't match the journal
- `drizzle-kit generate` asking nonsensical questions about column renames

## Fix Process

---

### Step 1: Checkout upstream/main

Switch to upstream/main to get a clean database state:

```bash
git checkout upstream/main
```

---

### Step 2: Apply migrations to database

Run the migration command:

```bash
bun --bun --cwd packages/db drizzle-kit migrate
```

---

### Step 3: Switch back to feature branch

Switch back to the feature branch:

```bash
git checkout <branch-name>
```

---

### Step 4: Clean up migration artifacts

Run cleanup commands:

```bash
# Identify what needs cleanup by checking diff
git diff upstream/main --stat -- packages/db/drizzle/

# Check current journal state
cat packages/db/drizzle/meta/_journal.json | tail -20
```

Then perform cleanup:
- Remove migration SQL files the branch added: `rm packages/db/drizzle/0010_*.sql`
- Remove corresponding snapshots: `rm packages/db/drizzle/meta/0010_snapshot.json`
- Restore journal from upstream: `git checkout upstream/main -- packages/db/drizzle/meta/_journal.json`
- Restore any accidentally modified snapshots: `git checkout upstream/main -- packages/db/drizzle/meta/0009_snapshot.json`
- Restore schema files that should match upstream (files user didn't intentionally modify)

---

### Step 5: Verify clean state

Run verification:

```bash
git diff upstream/main --stat -- packages/db/
```

The diff should now show ONLY schema file changes (e.g., `sessions.ts`), not migration files.

---

### Step 6: reseet database state

Ask the user (DO NOT DO THIS YOURSELF UNLESS YOU ARE ASKED TO DO SO) to reset the database state to the upstream/main state.

```bash
# reset the database volumes
docker compose down -v && docker compose up -d

# then seed the existing migrations
bun --bun --cwd packages/db drizzle-kit migrate
```

This will delete all data in the local database and re-apply the upstream migrations.

---

### Step 7: Regenerate migration

Generate a fresh migration for the schema changes:

```bash
bun run db:migrations:generate
```

This should create a new migration file (e.g., `0010_something.sql`) with just the changes.

---

### Step 8: Apply migration locally

Apply the new migration to the local database:

```bash
bun --bun --cwd packages/db drizzle-kit migrate
```

---

### Step 9: Verify and commit

After migration succeeds, verify:

```bash
# Check the final diff
git diff upstream/main --stat -- packages/db/

# Run typecheck
bun run typecheck

# Run tests
bun --bun run test
```

The diff should show:
- The new migration SQL file
- The new snapshot JSON
- Updated journal
- Schema file changes

## Troubleshooting

### If drizzle-kit asks about column renames during generate

The schema doesn't match what drizzle expects. Check if:
- Schema files were accidentally reverted during rebase
- Upstream renamed columns that your schema still has with old names

Fix: `git checkout upstream/main -- packages/db/src/tables/<file>.ts` for files you didn't intend to modify.

### If journal still has duplicates after cleanup

The checkout didn't work or there are staged changes. Run:
```bash
git checkout upstream/main -- packages/db/drizzle/meta/_journal.json
```

### If local DB is in weird state

Run migrate on upstream/main again, then switch back to branch.

## Key Files Reference

- `packages/db/drizzle/*.sql` - Migration SQL files (sequential: 0000, 0001, ...)
- `packages/db/drizzle/meta/_journal.json` - Tracks all migrations and their order
- `packages/db/drizzle/meta/NNNN_snapshot.json` - Schema snapshot after each migration
- `packages/db/src/tables/*.ts` - Drizzle schema definitions

## Commands Reference (for agent)

```bash
# All commands are non-interactive and safe for agent to run:
git diff upstream/main --stat -- packages/db/
git show upstream/main:packages/db/drizzle/meta/_journal.json
cat packages/db/drizzle/meta/_journal.json
ls packages/db/drizzle/*.sql
git checkout upstream/main -- <file>  # restore specific file
rm packages/db/drizzle/0010_*.sql     # cleanup
bun run db:migrations:generate
bun --bun --cwd packages/db drizzle-kit migrate
```

content:
--- name: storybook description: | ACTIVATE when creating storybook stories, reviewing PRs with .stories.tsx files, or planning Storybook-related work with rpi:* skills. --- # Storybook Component Taxonomy This skill defines the three-tier component taxonomy for Storybook stories and the patterns to follow. ## Component Taxonomy | Type | Definition | In Storybook? | |------|------------|---------------| | **Pure** | Stateless or low-state production component with no app stores, queries, routing, or providers | Yes — default | | **ShellDemo** | Storybook-only wrapper that composes real components to demonstrate interactivity, layouts, or state | Yes — sparingly | | **Wired** | Production component connected to business logic, hotkeys, stores, queries | No | ### Pure/Wired Production Pattern `Wired*` is the only prefix for connected production components. `Connected*` is retired repo-wide. A Wired component owns queries, stores, routing, hotkeys, and business logic, then composes Pure shells and leaves. Storybook interaction wrappers are always named `*ShellDemo`, never `Wired*`. Avoid prop-forwarding pure intermediates. A Pure layout component exposes literal `children`; the Wired layer fills those slots with Wired leaves, and each Wired leaf renders its Pure leaf with a flat, one-hop interface. The canonical production/story pairs are: - `KanbanBoard` / `WiredKanbanCard` - the shell kit in `packages/ui/src/components/sidebar/` / `WiredSidebarTaskTree`, `WiredTaskRow`, and `WiredSessionRow` - `ArtifactCommentPanel` / `WiredCommentThread`, using keyed children and `NEW_COMMENT_KEY` Stories use the same Pure shells as production and fill their slots with Pure leaves. They are provider-free. Never render or wrap a Wired component in a story. Pure composition has one seam: literal `children`. Do not add named `ReactNode` props, component props, or render props for Storybook convenience. When a shell must associate caller content with its own layout records, use keyed children, following `ArtifactCommentPanel`. ## Anti-Pattern: Mock-ups **Mock-up** — defines fake inline UI instead of importing real production components. These create noise and mislead developers about what's real vs. prototype. DELETE mock-ups; do not convert them. **Smell test:** The story file defines JSX/markup inline instead of importing a component from a production path like `../components/` or `@humanlayer/ui`. ## Story Patterns ### 1. Pure Story — Static Args (Default) The preferred form. Import the real Pure component and pass static data via `args`. ```tsx // packages/ui/src/components/session-label-badge.stories.tsx import type { Meta, StoryObj } from "@storybook/react" import { SessionLabelBadge } from "./session-label-badge" const meta = { title: "Components/SessionLabelBadge", component: SessionLabelBadge, } satisfies Meta export default meta type Story = StoryObj export const Default: Story = { args: { label: "bug-fix", color: "blue" }, } ``` ### 2. ShellDemo — Inline Wrapper for Interactivity For Pure components needing demo-only interactivity (dialogs, toggles), define a small provider-free `*ShellDemo` inside the `.stories.tsx`. The ShellDemo owns local state; the real Pure component is imported from production. ```tsx // packages/ui/src/components/bypass-permissions-dialog.stories.tsx const BypassPermissionsDialogShellDemo = ({ sessionCount }: { sessionCount?: number }) => { const [open, setOpen] = useState(false) return ( <> console.log("Confirmed with timeout:", minutes)} sessionCount={sessionCount} /> ) } export const Default: Story = { render: () => , } ``` ### 3. ShellDemo — Companion File for Complex Composition When a ShellDemo needs significant local state or composes multiple real Pure components, put it in `storybook/*.tsx`. Keep the `.stories.tsx` thin. ShellDemos remain provider-free; if a component requires app providers, story the Pure shells and leaves below that boundary instead. ```tsx // storybook/session-table.tsx — ShellDemo companion export const SessionTableShellDemo: FC = (props) => { const [selectedId, setSelectedId] = useState() return } // storybook/session-table.stories.tsx — thin const meta: Meta = { title: "Shell Demos/SessionTable", component: SessionTableShellDemo, } export const Default: Story = { args: {} } ``` ### 4. ShellDemo — Page Layout Composition (Rare) For demonstrating page layouts or how multiple real components sit together. Use sparingly. ```tsx import { SidebarShell, TaskRow } from "@humanlayer/ui" export const WithTask: Story = { render: () => (
    Pure session rows go here
 ), } ``` `KanbanBoard.stories.tsx`, the sidebar stories, and the artifact-comment-panel stories are the canonical slot-composition examples. Their shells are production components, their slot contents are Pure leaves, and none requires an app provider. ## ShellDemo Nav Group All ShellDemos must use the `Shell Demos/` top-level nav group prefix in their `title` to visually separate them from Pure component stories: ```tsx const meta = { title: "Shell Demos/SessionTable", // NOT "Components/SessionTable" component: SessionTableDemo, } ``` ## Quick Checklist Before creating or approving a story: 1. Does the story import a real production component? If no → DELETE or fix 2. Does the story render only Pure components and stay provider-free? If no → move down to the Pure boundary 3. Does composition use only literal `children` (keyed when matching layout records)? If no → fix the production seam 4. Does the demo add local interaction state? Name it `*ShellDemo`; complex state → companion file in `.../storybook/` 5. Is the `title` correct? ShellDemos → `Shell Demos/...`; Pure → `Components/...` or existing group ## Locations - `packages/ui/src/` — shared component library stories (port 6006) - `apps/riptide-ui/src/` — app-specific stories (port 6007) - `apps/riptide-ui/storybook/` companion directories for complex ShellDemo wrappers - `packages/ui/storybook/` companion directories for complex ShellDemo wrappers ## Running Storybook ```bash cd packages/ui && bun --bun run storybook # port 6006 cd apps/riptide-ui && bun --bun run storybook # port 6007 ```

name: stripe-billing-verification
description: Run Stripe webhook smoke tests and billing lifecycle simulations for stripe
content:
---
name: stripe-billing-verification
description: Run Stripe webhook smoke tests and billing lifecycle simulations for stripe
---

## Task

Default to Stripe CLI forwarding for local work. Use ngrok only when the user specifically needs Stripe to deliver to a public HTTPS endpoint.

## Quick Reference

```bash
export STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET="$(stripe listen --print-secret | tr -d '\r\n')"
LISTENER_LOG=/tmp/stripe-billing-verification/stripe-listen.log
mkdir -p "$(dirname "$LISTENER_LOG")"
stripe listen --forward-to http://localhost:8700/webhooks/stripe \
  2>&1 | tee "$LISTENER_LOG"
stripe trigger payment_intent.succeeded
stripe trigger customer.subscription.created
```

```bash
curl -i http://localhost:8700/webhooks/stripe \
  -X POST \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{}'
```

```bash
stripe test_helpers test_clocks create --frozen-time <unix-ts>
stripe test_helpers test_clocks advance <clock-id> --frozen-time <unix-ts>
```

## Workflow

1. Ensure local `riptide-api` is running on `http://localhost:8700`
2. Capture the CLI forwarding secret with `stripe listen --print-secret`
3. Export that value as `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET`
4. Start a separate `stripe listen --forward-to http://localhost:8700/webhooks/stripe` process and tee its output to a file so the initial readiness output is preserved even though the process stays attached by design
5. Trigger smoke-test events with `stripe trigger ...`
6. For lifecycle validation, create a fresh Test Clock, attach a fresh customer, advance the clock, and wait for readiness before asserting results

## Secret Rules

- `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET` must match the delivery path in use
- Stripe CLI forwarding uses a transient CLI session secret
- Dashboard or Workbench endpoints use that endpoint's signing secret
- these secrets are not interchangeable
- if a signature check fails, first verify that the configured secret matches the traffic source

`stripe listen --print-secret` is the preferred non-interactive way to capture the local forwarding secret because it prints only the secret and exits. It does not keep the listener running.

## Captured Output and Dev Logs

When starting the long-running Stripe listener, always tee its output to a file so you keep the immediate readiness lines and forwarded event feedback:

```bash
LISTENER_LOG=/tmp/stripe-billing-verification/stripe-listen.log
mkdir -p "$(dirname "$LISTENER_LOG")"
stripe listen --forward-to http://localhost:8700/webhooks/stripe \
  2>&1 | tee "$LISTENER_LOG"
```

- the command hangs by design because the listener stays attached
- `tee` keeps the live terminal output visible and also saves it for later inspection
- after triggering events, inspect `"$LISTENER_LOG"` to confirm forwarding, event ids, and response codes

Riptide dev logs live in:

```bash
~/.humanlayer/riptide/logs/
```

To list recent dev logs:

```bash
ls -tr -la ~/.humanlayer/riptide/logs/ | tail -n 10
```

- look for `riptide-daemon-dev-...` files when checking daemon-side errors
- look for `riptide-api-dev-...` files when checking webhook handler behavior
- use those files to verify accepted events or fetch stack traces and Stripe-related errors after a smoke test

## Smoke-Test Procedure

1. Export the CLI forwarding secret:

```bash
export STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET="$(stripe listen --print-secret | tr -d '\r\n')"
```

2. Start forwarding in a separate terminal:

```bash
LISTENER_LOG=/tmp/stripe-billing-verification/stripe-listen.log
mkdir -p "$(dirname "$LISTENER_LOG")"
stripe listen --forward-to http://localhost:8700/webhooks/stripe \
  2>&1 | tee "$LISTENER_LOG"
```

3. Confirm unsigned traffic fails with `400`:

```bash
curl -i http://localhost:8700/webhooks/stripe \
  -X POST \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{}'
```

4. Trigger one or more smoke events:

```bash
stripe trigger payment_intent.succeeded
stripe trigger customer.subscription.created
stripe trigger customer.subscription.updated
```

5. Verify that the route returns `2xx` for valid signed events and that logs include event id and type.

If you need to confirm the webhook made it through the rest of the local stack, also check the latest files in `~/.humanlayer/riptide/logs/`.

## Test Clock Workflow

Use Test Clocks for time-based billing scenarios in Stripe test mode.

- create a fresh Test Clock
- create a fresh customer attached to that clock
- create the subscription or other billing object for that customer
- advance time in steps
- wait for the clock to reach `ready`
- inspect resulting webhook traffic and Stripe object state

Important constraints:

- Checkout and Test Clocks are separate workflows in Phase 2
- Test Clocks work best with newly created customers
- renewal-related events can require advancing slightly beyond the nominal boundary because invoice finalization may lag
- if webhook acknowledgement fails, Stripe can delay lifecycle side effects

## Safe Automation Guidance

Safe to automate:

- capturing the CLI forwarding secret with `stripe listen --print-secret`
- starting and stopping local Stripe CLI forwarding
- teeing Stripe CLI listener output to a persistent file for later inspection
- sending `stripe trigger` smoke events
- polling Test Clock readiness
- explaining the correct secret-selection flow
- reading `~/.humanlayer/riptide/logs/` to confirm daemon or API-side errors

Keep manual or human-confirmed:

- Stripe Dashboard or Workbench endpoint setup
- copying endpoint signing secrets from the Dashboard
- validating a public ngrok endpoint in the Stripe UI
- decisions about which real environment endpoint to exercise

## Troubleshooting

### Invalid signature

Check whether:

- `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET` matches the active delivery path
- the API was restarted after the env change
- the listener and `--print-secret` used the same Stripe account and mode
- the route verified the untouched raw body rather than parsed JSON

### `stripe listen --print-secret` succeeded, but forwarding does not happen

That is expected. Start the long-running listener separately:

```bash
LISTENER_LOG=/tmp/stripe-billing-verification/stripe-listen.log
mkdir -p "$(dirname "$LISTENER_LOG")"
stripe listen --forward-to http://localhost:8700/webhooks/stripe \
  2>&1 | tee "$LISTENER_LOG"
```

### Need daemon or API errors after the trigger

List recent dev logs and inspect the newest `-dev-` file for the component you need:

```bash
ls -tr -la ~/.humanlayer/riptide/logs/ | tail -n 10
```

Use `riptide-daemon-dev-...` for daemon issues and `riptide-api-dev-...` for webhook-route issues.

### `stripe trigger` does not match a real billing flow

That is also expected. `stripe trigger` is for smoke testing route acceptance and basic event intake. Use Test Clocks for lifecycle progression.

## References

- `docs/stripe-billing-webhook-testing.md`
- `.claude/skills/stripe-billing-verification/references/cli-and-test-clocks.md`

name: subagent-orchestrator
description: orchestrate sub-agents to accomplish complex long-horizon tasks without losing coherency by delegating to sub-agents
---

This skill provides you with **CRITICAL** instructions that will help you to maintain coherency in long-horizon context-heavy tasks. 

You have a large number of tools available to you. The most important one is the one that allows you to dispatch sub-agents: either `Agent` or `Task`. 

All non-trivial operations should be delegated to sub-agents. You should delegate research and codebase understanding tasks to codebase-analyzer, codebase-locator and pattern-locator sub-agents. 

You should delegate running bash commands (particularly ones that are likely to produce lots of output) such as investigating with the `aws` CLI, using the `gh` CLI, digging through logs to `Bash` sub-agents. 

You should use separate sub-agents for separate tasks, and you may launch them in parallel - but do not delegate multiple tasks that are likely to have significant overlap to separate sub-agents.

IMPORTANT: if the user has already given you a task, you should proceed with that task using this approach. 

If you have not already been explicitly given a taks, you should ask the user what task they would like for you to work on - do not assume or begin working on a ticket autoatically.

---
name: test-it-locally
description: Test Riptide changes against the local devstack through the UI, HumanLayer CLI, and database. Use for local verification, agent-browser checks, local task or session creation, and devstack setup.
---

# Test It Locally

Test the changed behavior and its stored state, not just whether the app loads.

### Workflow

1. Inspect the worktree stack. Read the whole plaintext output: it includes the local WorkOS organization, routes, ports, logs, generated env state, and an API health line. Sync only if it is missing or stale; `--compose --seed` is usually already done, then run `status` again.

```bash
bun --bun run devstack status
bun --bun run devstack sync --compose --seed
```

2. Use the `API healthcheck` line from the full `bun --bun run devstack status` output. `passed` means the app stack is ready; `failed` means it is not running.

3. If it failed, start Riptide in a tmux session that excludes the parent daemon's identity. This keeps the initial process and any later panes on the devstack's local identity. Use `riptide:native` only when the native shell matters.

```bash
STACK_ID="$(bun --bun run devstack status --json | jq -r '.id')" && \
TMUX_SESSION="riptide-$STACK_ID" && \
tmux new-session -d -s "$TMUX_SESSION" -c "$PWD" \
  "env -u DAEMON_IDENTITY -u RIPTIDE_DAEMON_EXPECTED_IDENTITY bun --bun run riptide" && \
tmux set-environment -u -t "$TMUX_SESSION" DAEMON_IDENTITY && \
tmux set-environment -u -t "$TMUX_SESSION" RIPTIDE_DAEMON_EXPECTED_IDENTITY
tmux attach -t "$TMUX_SESSION"
```

Do not use `tmux set-environment -gu`; the tmux server is shared by other devstacks.

4. Open the worktree URL headless with a browser session and profile keyed by the devstack ID. The named session isolates the running agent-browser daemon, while the profile persists cookies, IndexedDB, and cache. Both are needed so multiple devstacks can run browser checks in parallel without sharing state. Do not use `--session-name`, the fixed `riptide` profile, or a fixed localhost port.

```bash
DEVSTACK_STATUS="$(bun --bun run devstack status --json)" && \
export DEVSTACK_ID="$(jq -r '.id' <<<"$DEVSTACK_STATUS")" && \
export AGENT_BROWSER_SESSION="riptide-$DEVSTACK_ID" && \
export AGENT_BROWSER_PROFILE="$HOME/.agent-browser/profiles/riptide-$DEVSTACK_ID" && \
APP_URL="$(jq -r '.routes.ui' <<<"$DEVSTACK_STATUS")" && \
agent-browser open "$APP_URL" && agent-browser wait --load networkidle && agent-browser get url && agent-browser snapshot -i
```

Set `AGENT_BROWSER_SESSION` and `AGENT_BROWSER_PROFILE` from status at the start of each new shell call that runs agent-browser. All agent-browser commands in that call then target only this devstack. Do not run an unscoped `agent-browser close`, because it closes the default session rather than this stack's session.

If this shows WorkOS login, use the shared sandbox test user from the root `.env`. Read the values without printing them, and refer to them by variable name in every `agent-browser` command. Never put a credential value in a command, response, screenshot, log, or committed file.

```bash
set -a
source .env
set +a
DEVSTACK_STATUS="$(bun --bun run devstack status --json)" && \
export DEVSTACK_ID="$(jq -r '.id' <<<"$DEVSTACK_STATUS")" && \
export AGENT_BROWSER_SESSION="riptide-$DEVSTACK_ID" && \
export AGENT_BROWSER_PROFILE="$HOME/.agent-browser/profiles/riptide-$DEVSTACK_ID" && \
test -n "$DEVSTACK_LOCAL_USER_EMAIL" && test -n "$DEVSTACK_LOCAL_USER_PASSWORD"
```

Source `.env` rather than extracting values with `grep` and `cut`. Shell parsing removes valid
wrapping quotes; text extraction keeps those quotes and sends them as part of the credential.

Snapshot the login page before entering credentials. WorkOS can show the fields on one screen or ask for email first and password second. Use labels and roles instead of refs after entering the email so later snapshots do not print it:

```bash
set -a
source .env
set +a
DEVSTACK_STATUS="$(bun --bun run devstack status --json)" && \
export DEVSTACK_ID="$(jq -r '.id' <<<"$DEVSTACK_STATUS")" && \
export AGENT_BROWSER_SESSION="riptide-$DEVSTACK_ID" && \
export AGENT_BROWSER_PROFILE="$HOME/.agent-browser/profiles/riptide-$DEVSTACK_ID" && \
test -n "$DEVSTACK_LOCAL_USER_EMAIL" && test -n "$DEVSTACK_LOCAL_USER_PASSWORD" && \
agent-browser find label "Email" fill "$DEVSTACK_LOCAL_USER_EMAIL"
agent-browser find role button click --name "Continue with email"
agent-browser wait --url "**/password**"
agent-browser find label "Password" fill "$DEVSTACK_LOCAL_USER_PASSWORD"
agent-browser find role button click --name "Sign in"
```

If WorkOS asks for an organization, select the exact name shown by the `Local organization` line from `bun --bun run devstack status`. The WorkOS ID in parentheses can disambiguate matching names. Any configured sandbox or dev organization is valid; do not assume a fixed name or ID. Wait for the app URL, then snapshot the signed-in page. The shared profile keeps the resulting session for later runs. If login fails, collect the URL and browser errors, but do not snapshot or take a screenshot after entering either credential.

If either variable is missing, do not ask the user to send credentials in chat. Ask them to add the shared test account values to the root `.env`, or use the headed fallback below when the shared account itself needs repair:

```bash
DEVSTACK_STATUS="$(bun --bun run devstack status --json)" && \
export DEVSTACK_ID="$(jq -r '.id' <<<"$DEVSTACK_STATUS")" && \
export AGENT_BROWSER_SESSION="riptide-$DEVSTACK_ID" && \
export AGENT_BROWSER_PROFILE="$HOME/.agent-browser/profiles/riptide-$DEVSTACK_ID" && \
APP_URL="$(jq -r '.routes.ui' <<<"$DEVSTACK_STATUS")" && \
agent-browser close && agent-browser --headed open "$APP_URL"
# user logs in
agent-browser close
agent-browser open "$APP_URL" && agent-browser wait --load networkidle && agent-browser snapshot -i
```

Read [references/shared-test-user.md](references/shared-test-user.md) when setting up, rotating, or repairing the shared account.

5. Exercise the exact flow. Snapshot before each action, use `@eN` refs, and resnapshot after every page or DOM change. Check the UI result and the API or database end state.

```bash
DEVSTACK_STATUS="$(bun --bun run devstack status --json)" && \
export DEVSTACK_ID="$(jq -r '.id' <<<"$DEVSTACK_STATUS")" && \
export AGENT_BROWSER_SESSION="riptide-$DEVSTACK_ID" && \
export AGENT_BROWSER_PROFILE="$HOME/.agent-browser/profiles/riptide-$DEVSTACK_ID" && \
agent-browser snapshot -i
agent-browser click @e1
agent-browser snapshot -i
agent-browser screenshot "/tmp/riptide-$DEVSTACK_ID-local.png"
```

On failure, set the stack-scoped session and profile in the same shell call, then run `agent-browser get url`, `agent-browser errors`, `agent-browser console`, and take a stack-scoped screenshot. Close only this stack's session when done:

```bash
DEVSTACK_STATUS="$(bun --bun run devstack status --json)" && \
export DEVSTACK_ID="$(jq -r '.id' <<<"$DEVSTACK_STATUS")" && \
export AGENT_BROWSER_SESSION="riptide-$DEVSTACK_ID" && \
export AGENT_BROWSER_PROFILE="$HOME/.agent-browser/profiles/riptide-$DEVSTACK_ID" && \
agent-browser get url && agent-browser errors && agent-browser console && \
agent-browser screenshot "/tmp/riptide-$DEVSTACK_ID-failure.png"

agent-browser close
```

### Devstack

`status` reports the stack ID, configured local organization name and WorkOS ID, routes, ports, log directory, generated env state, and API health. `sync --compose --seed` allocates the worktree stack, starts service containers, runs migrations, and seeds the local org. Use `bun --bun run devstack help` for other commands.

Read more if needed: [references/devstack.md](references/devstack.md).

### agent-browser

Always set both `AGENT_BROWSER_SESSION=riptide-<devstack-id>` and `AGENT_BROWSER_PROFILE=~/.agent-browser/profiles/riptide-<devstack-id>` before agent-browser commands. `AGENT_BROWSER_SESSION` isolates the live daemon used by concurrent agents. `AGENT_BROWSER_PROFILE` persists the stack's cookies, IndexedDB, and cache across restarts. `--session-name` does not replace either one. A new devstack route may still need a fresh WorkOS login, so use the shared test user flow above instead of opening a headed browser. Refs expire after page changes. Use `eval --stdin` for complex JavaScript or CSS injection.

Read more if needed: [`.claude/skills/agent-browser/SKILL.md`](../agent-browser/SKILL.md), [`.claude/skills/agent-browser/references/commands.md`](../agent-browser/references/commands.md), [`.claude/skills/agent-browser/references/authentication.md`](../agent-browser/references/authentication.md), and [`.claude/skills/agent-browser/references/snapshot-refs.md`](../agent-browser/references/snapshot-refs.md).

### Local CLI testing

The root `.env` loads through Bun. Set this worktree's dynamic routes, then use `apps/cli` with `--dev`:

```bash
export DEV_API_ORIGIN="$(bun --bun run devstack status --json | jq -r '.routes.api')"
export DEV_SYNC_ORIGIN="$(bun --bun run devstack status --json | jq -r '.routes.sync')"
bun --bun apps/cli/src/index.ts --dev login
bun --bun apps/cli/src/index.ts --dev api sync online-hosts --limit 5
```

Create a task, upload its ticket, and launch a session with IDs from prior output:

```bash
bun --bun apps/cli/src/index.ts --dev api tasks create --name "Task Name" --slug "task-slug" --default-working-directory "$PWD" --workflow-type outline_only --worktree-timing later
bun --bun apps/cli/src/index.ts --dev api uploads upsert-text --task-id "TASK_ID" --file-name "ticket.md" --content "Ticket content here"
bun --bun apps/cli/src/index.ts --dev api sessions launch --task-id '"TASK_ID"' --title '"Session Title"' --text "use the rpi:create-structure-outline skill" --working-directory "$PWD" --host-id "HOST_ID" --coding-agent claude --provider anthropic --model haiku --permissions-mode bypass
bun --bun apps/cli/src/index.ts --dev api sync sessions --task-id "TASK_ID" --limit 10
```

Workflow types: `rpi`, `outline_only`, `prd_tdd`, `oneshot`, or omit for freeform. Worktree timing: `now`, `later`, `never`.

Verify stored state directly when useful:

```bash
docker compose exec postgres psql -U postgres electric -c "SELECT s.id, s.status, t.workflow_type, t.worktree_timing FROM sessions s JOIN tasks t ON t.id = s.task_id WHERE s.id = 'SESSION_ID';"
```

Read more if needed: [references/local-cli-testing/SKILL.md](references/local-cli-testing/SKILL.md).

### Durable Streams Testing

The devstack will have a durable streams server running that streams for token streaming and `diff-files` and `diff-patches` are written to for the sync diff system.

While the code paths hit the durable streams server through the auth proxy because that is how code is forced to reach it in production, for local testing it is ok to request against the durable streams server directly.

TO do so you should understand what route is provided for the stream read/write or in the streamDB collection, and understand how the riptide-electric-proxy maps that to a URL on the durable stream server.

The durable stream server can be interacted with programmatically using the durable streams CLI `@durable-streams/cli` which it is safe to be a dev dependency in the top-level package.json.

Reference: https://durablestreams.com/cli

`npx @durable-streams/cli <command> [option]` or `durable-streams <command> [option]`

- `--url <url>` - stream server URL
- `--auth` - not applicable
- `--json` - usually what we're looking at, shorthasnd for `--content-type application/json`

Read the webpage for detailed usage and subcommands - e.g. `create`, `read`, `write`
